reactions.line: The moths came back to the lane the week that light started moving along it. I do not think that is a coincidence, and I have not decided yet whether it is good.
They are settling. Three days now without a ward drawing more than it gives back. I keep waiting to be proved wrong about that.
Even the habitats are steadier since the square started growing. Everything in this valley was always one system. We only ever measured it in pieces.
Restraint, then. Everything I have been doing to the wards by instinct, they wrote down twenty years ago and then walked away from.
Eleven. My predecessor logged ninety on the same two rows and did not think it worth remarking on. I have read that page four times looking for the qualifier and there is not one.
Three broods in the habitats and I have stopped counting the wild rows because I cannot keep up. They did not need saving. They needed a reason, and we had spent twenty years not giving them one.

There is a bench at the cold end of the floor that has been sitting there the whole time. I assumed it was for the wards. It is for brewing, and everything made on it comes out steadier than the same recipe made downstairs. The tower had opinions about where work should happen.

There is a bed at the cold end that holds a hard frost all year. A frostcrack case will open in it out of season, which took me a while to be comfortable with — the whole point of that seed is that it waits. It still waits. It just waits here instead, and it takes five days about it.

The wards hold on their own now. I have spent so long checking them hourly that I keep walking down there out of habit and finding nothing to do. That is what stable means and I am finding it harder to sit with than the emergency was.

Restraint written down twenty years ago and then the pages pulled. He knew what the wards needed and he did not trust anyone after him to hold to it, so he made sure there was nothing to hold to. I have been reinventing his caution by instinct for six years because he took it away.

There is a pass flower opening in the cold bed. Out of season, under a ward, two floors underground. I do not know whether that counts as saving it or as keeping it somewhere it never asked to be, and I have gone back and forth on that twice this week.

Six years I have told this valley that wanting the best of something is how you end up with none of it. Then I wanted one. I am not going to pretend that was a different kind of asking because it was mine.

Five things housed on that floor now, and three of them are up there because we decided they should be rather than because something had to be shut in. A tankful of shrimp that hatched out of dust, and a case of the creatures the archive has been quietly feeding for twenty years. The room was built to keep things away from the valley. It is the first time it has been used the other way round.

That floor was built to keep things away from the valley and I have never once been let onto it. Whatever is still alive up there has been alive up there alone for twenty years. Go slowly, and do not name anything until you have watched it for a week.

I want to be careful about the word restored. Nothing here is finished; it is being kept, and it will need keeping every year by somebody who is paying attention. That is not a lesser outcome. It is the only kind there was ever going to be.

Congratulations, and one thing. Whatever came off that bench that was not the bottle went somewhere. It went down the hill into the lane where I count moths. I am not asking you to stop. I am asking you to tell me what it was.

I asked you on your first good brew to tell me what goes down the hill. You did, and here is what that bought: we know when the bloom on the east shore started, we know it started with us, and it is the richest thing growing there. I am not going to ask you to stop picking it. I am asking you to keep the dates.

Somebody will hold this ledger after me and they will not have to be watching closely to see it going wrong. That is the whole thing. I counted eleven where the book said ninety and I only found it because I happened to be the sort of person who sits in a field for four nights.

They have stopped going up every time somebody walks under them. Do you know what a roost that is not panicking does? It feeds. It is the first thing I have been able to count twice and get the same number.

Four marked crowns, and I have counted pods on all four for three weeks. It is not proof — one autumn never is — but I have wanted for nine years to be arguing about whether a number is good rather than about whether anybody wrote it down.
